name: The mind's mechanisms
draftedBy: Claude, 15 Nov 2026, from Bryan's words the same day: "sunk cost fallacies cognitive dissonance et cetera ... people don't know how these affect things. why: Your mind runs on shortcuts. Most of the time they help. Some of them cost you money, time and years, and the people selling to you know them better than you do.

units.title: Sunk cost
units.outcome: Spot the sunk cost trap, and choose by what is ahead instead of what is already spent.
units.why: Money, time and effort you already spent are gone whichever way you choose. Letting them pick for you means paying again for something already lost.
units.reachesYou: The car you keep fixing, the job you stay in because of the years you put in, the course you finish though it stopped helping, the plate you clean though you are full.
units.do: Pick one thing you keep doing mostly because of what you already put in. Ask: if I were starting fresh today, with nothing spent, would I choose this? Write the answer down.

scene.analogy: Staying through a bad movie because you paid
map: paying again for what is gone

actors.label: "I paid for it, so I'll stay."

beats.say: Thirty minutes in, it is bad.
The only real choice: what comes next.

film.label: The bad deal
film.sub: the job, the car, the plan

beats.say: Spent is spent. Choose what's ahead.

units.title: Cognitive dissonance
units.outcome: Notice when you are changing the story to stop a clash, instead of changing what you do.
units.why: When two of your thoughts clash, like "I chose well" and "this is not working", it feels bad. The fastest way to stop the feeling is to change the story. The fact stays where it was.
units.reachesYou: Defending a car, a candidate, a partner or a plan long after it stopped working, because admitting it would mean you chose wrong.
units.do: Find one thing you defend a little too hard. Say out loud: "I chose that, and it is not working." Notice the sting, and notice that nothing bad happened.

scene.analogy: New shoes that pinch, called comfy
map: the fact that it is not working
the story that stops the clash

beats.say: So you change the story, not the shoes.

shoe.label: Your choice
shoe.sub: a plan, a vote, a buy

beats.say: Fix the shoe, not the story.

units.title: Fear of missing out
units.outcome: Feel the pull of "only today" and "everyone is going", and still take the time to choose.
units.why: A closing door makes anything look more valuable. Sellers and apps close doors on purpose, so you decide before you think.
units.reachesYou: "Sale ends tonight", "only 2 left", countdown timers, the group chat everyone is in, scrolling at 2 AM so you don't miss a post.
units.do: Next time something says "only today", wait one day. Write down whether you still want it, and whether the deal really ended.

map: buying what you did not need
the deal that always comes back

beats.say: The elevator doors start to close.
Sales and feeds work the same way.

units.title: Confirmation bias
units.outcome: Look for what would prove you wrong, not only for what agrees with you.
units.why: Once you believe something, you look where it will be confirmed and skip where it might not. Each look feels like proof. It is the same room, searched again.
units.reachesYou: The feed that only shows what you already like, the friend you ask because you know their answer, the reviews you read only after you bought it.
units.do: Pick one thing you are sure of. Find the best case against it, written by someone who knows the subject. Read it to the end before you answer it.

scene.analogy: Searching for your keys only where you hope they are

beats.say: You search it. Again. And again.
They were in your coat all along.
Look where you hope it isn't.

units.title: Anchoring
units.outcome: Notice when the first number you heard is setting the price, and set your own first.
units.why: The first number you hear becomes the ruler you measure everything after it with, even when that number was made up. Sellers say theirs first for a reason.
units.reachesYou: Car stickers, "was $90", the first offer in a raise talk, a hospital bill you negotiate down, a home's asking price.
units.do: Before your next big purchase or pay talk, write down what you think it is worth, from your own research, before you hear their number.

scene.analogy: Haggling down from the sticker on a car

beats.say: The first number pulls every number after it.

units.title: Loss aversion
units.outcome: Weigh a possible loss and an equal gain on the same scale.
units.why: Losing something hurts about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good. So people pass up good chances to avoid small risks, and hold on to bad ones to avoid admitting a loss.
units.reachesYou: Staying in a job you have outgrown, keeping a stock that keeps falling, buying the extended warranty, "free trial" offers that count on you hating to lose what you already have.
units.do: Think of one change you keep putting off. Write the best thing that could come of it and the worst. Read them as the same size. Which is bigger now?

map: how much more a loss weighs

beats.say: Same money. The loss hurts about twice as much.
So you dodge risks you should take.
Jobs, moves, money: the same scale.

units.title: Availability
units.outcome: Tell how often something happens from how easy it is to picture.
units.why: Your mind judges how likely something is by how fast an example comes to mind. Loud, rare, scary things come to mind fast. Quiet, common dangers do not.
units.reachesYou: Fearing planes but not cars, buying lottery tickets after a winner is on the news, worrying about strangers while the real risks sit at home: the stairs, the pool, the car.
units.do: Pick one thing you worry about. Look up how many people it actually hurts in a year, then look up one ordinary thing you do daily. Compare the two numbers.

scene.analogy: Afraid of sharks, not the drive to the beach
map: the danger that is easy to picture

beats.say: A shark attack is on the news. All week.
You drive there without a thought.
The drive is the real danger.
Check the numbers, not the noise.

units.title: Bandwagon
units.outcome: Tell "many people chose it" apart from "it is good".
units.why: A crowd is a quick signal, and sometimes a good one. But a line can form just because there was already a line. Then nobody in it actually checked.
units.reachesYou: The stock everyone is buying at the top, the viral product, the opinion your whole group switched to in a week, five-star counts bought in bulk.
units.do: Next time you are drawn to something because it is popular, find one reason to want it that would still be true if nobody else wanted it.

scene.analogy: Picking the restaurant with the line

beats.say: Others see the line, and follow.
You join. It must be good.
B was better. Nobody tried it.
A line is not a review.

units.title: Status quo bias
units.outcome: Ask whether you would choose what you have if you were choosing today.
units.why: Whatever you already have feels safe, even when it costs more. Changing takes a small effort now; staying costs a little every month, quietly, forever.
units.reachesYou: Phone and internet plans, insurance, bank fees, the subscription you forgot, the default settings on every app, the retirement plan you never set up.
units.do: Pick one bill you have paid the same way for over a year. Spend ten minutes looking at what else is out there. Make the call if it is better.

beats.say: A plan for half the price shows up.
Every month you stay, you pay $40 more.

units.title: Framing
units.outcome: Say a fact the other way round before you decide on it.
units.why: The same fact can be wrapped as a gain or a loss, a "free" or a "fee", and your choice follows the wrapper. Whoever writes the label picks the wrapper.
units.reachesYou: "90% fat free", "only $1 a day", "95% success rate", "a 5% chance of failure", "tax relief", "death tax": the same numbers or the same law, sold or scared by the words.
units.do: Find one label, ad or headline this week and rewrite it the other way round ("90% fat free" to "10% fat"). Notice whether it still sells.

map: saying it the other way round

beats.say: You grab A. It sounds healthier.
Flip the label before you choose.

units.title: Reciprocity
units.outcome: Take a gift without letting it decide what you buy or agree to.
units.why: When someone gives you something, you feel you owe them. That feeling holds families and friendships together, and sellers use it on purpose with gifts that cost them little.
units.reachesYou: Free samples, free trials, the free pen and calendar from a charity before the ask, the "free" dinner at a timeshare talk, the favor before the favor.
units.do: Next time you get something free from someone selling, say thank you and decide as if you had not got it. Notice the pull while you do.

scene.analogy: The free sample at the cheese counter

beats.say: A smiling clerk hands you a free sample.
You eat it. It was free.
Now you feel you owe them.
You buy $24 of cheese you did not need.
Small gift, big ask: the same move.

smp.label: Small favor
smp.sub: free trial, a pen, a dinner

units.title: Authority
units.outcome: Trust what someone has shown, not what they wear or what they are called.
units.why: Following real experts saves time. But the signs of expertise, a coat, a title, a confident voice, are easy to wear, and people obey the signs even when the order is wrong.
units.reachesYou: Actors in white coats in ads, "doctor recommended", the caller who says they are from your bank or the IRS, a confident guest on TV speaking outside their field.
units.do: Next time someone is introduced as an expert, look up one thing they actually did in that field. If you cannot find one, treat the claim like anyone else's.

scene.analogy: The actor in a lab coat in an ad

beats.say: Someone in a lab coat, in an ad.
You trust the coat. You buy.
An actor. The coat is a costume.
Titles and uniforms work the same way.
Ask what they did, not what they wear.

units.title: Scarcity
units.outcome: Want a thing for what it is, not for how few seem to be left.
units.why: Things that seem rare feel more valuable, even when they are exactly the same. A seller can make anything seem rare with one line of text.
units.reachesYou: "Only 2 left in stock", "3 people are looking at this", limited drops, last seats at this price, the countdown on a checkout page.
units.do: Next time a page says "only a few left", screenshot it and check again tomorrow. Note whether the number really changed.

map: value from rarity, not from the thing

beats.say: A hat. 10 in stock. You shrug.
Limited drops, last seats: same counter.
Rare is not the same as good.

units.title: Hindsight bias
units.outcome: Remember what you really expected before you knew how it ended.
units.why: Once you know how something turned out, your memory quietly rewrites what you expected, so the past looks obvious. Then the future looks easier to call than it is.
units.reachesYou: "I knew that stock would crash", "I always said they would break up", blaming someone for missing what only looks obvious now, betting big on the next call.
units.do: Before the next game, election or big decision, write down what you expect and how sure you are. Read it after the result.

beats.say: Before the game: "Could go either way."
Your memory rewrites what you said.
So you bet big next time.
Write it down before you know.

units.title: Dunning-Kruger: knowing a little
units.outcome: Notice when being new at something is making you feel sure of it.
units.why: When you are new at something, you cannot yet see what you are missing, so it feels easy. As skill grows, so does the view of what is left to learn. Researchers argue about how big this effect is, but the pattern shows up often.
units.reachesYou: The new driver who speeds, the person who read one article and argues with doctors, the first-week trader, the new boss who changes everything on day one.
units.do: Pick one thing you feel sure about but learned recently. Find someone with years in it and ask them what beginners usually get wrong.

scene.analogy: The new driver who thinks they drive great
map: not yet seeing what you are missing
skill that shows how much is left

beats.say: A little skill feels like a lot.
Five years later: more skill, less sure.
Anything new works the same way.
Feeling sure is not the same as being good.

units.title: Planning fallacy
units.outcome: Plan from how long things really took before, not from how they should go.
units.why: When you plan, you picture the job going right. You do not picture the missing tape, the wrong part, the second coat. So almost every plan comes out too short and too cheap.
units.reachesYou: The repair that takes all weekend, the budget that runs out in week three, the move, the wedding, the road project that is years late and millions over.
units.do: Before your next project, find a time you did something like it. Use how long that really took as your estimate, then add a little.

map: the plan with nothing going wrong
the tape, the color, the second coat

beats.say: No tape. Run to the store.
Plan from how long it took last time.

units.title: Variable reward
units.outcome: Spot what keeps you pulling a lever that only pays now and then.
units.why: A reward that comes every time gets boring. A reward that comes at random keeps you pulling, because the next one might be the one. Slot machines are built on this, and so are many apps.
units.reachesYou: Pull-to-refresh, the feed you scroll past midnight, checking for likes, loot boxes in games, scratch-off tickets, refreshing your email.
units.do: Turn off the notifications for one app for a week. Notice how often your hand reaches for it anyway.

scene.analogy: A slot machine, and the pull-to-refresh on your phone
map: a like, a message, a new post

beats.say: Not knowing when it pays is the hook.
Your phone works the same way.
Feeds and games are built on this.

phone.label: The payout
phone.sub: a like, a message, a post

beats.say: Unhook it: turn the alerts off.

lab.title: The lever
lab.ask: Sit down at the machine and pull. Stay as long as it feels worth it, then walk away. Then try a machine that pays a different way, and compare what your own hand did.
lab.triesNote: tall is a coin, short is nothing, the line is where it stopped paying

rules.if: every pull pays, and one day it stops,
rules.then: the first empty pull tells you. Nothing was ever empty before, so you know it is over and walking away is easy.

rules.if: every third pull pays, and one day it stops,
rules.then: you had learned the beat. When the third pull comes up empty the beat is broken, and you can tell.

rules.if: it pays at random, and one day it stops,
rules.then: an empty pull tells you nothing. Empty pulls were normal all along, so "it is over" looks exactly like "almost". Look how far past the line this try goes. This is the machine that keeps a hand pulling.

map: the swipe, the refresh, the check
a like, a message, a new post
never knowing if the next one is the one
lab.meet: Where you meet this: pull to refresh. A feed that is only sometimes good. A game with a prize box. Someone who texts back only sometimes. None of them pay every time. A cheap reward that comes at random takes over a signal that was built for finding real things.

units.title: Halo effect
units.outcome: Judge each part of a person or product on its own, not by one bright feature.
units.why: One good trait, like looks, fame or a confident voice, glows over everything else. You end up trusting someone's honesty, skill or price because of their smile.
units.reachesYou: Celebrity ads, attractive people getting lighter sentences and better jobs, a slick website you trust with your card, a brand you like making a product you never checked.
units.do: Next time you like someone or something right away, list three things you are assuming about it. Check one.

map: judging the parts on their own

beats.say: One good trait starts to glow.
Honest? Seems so. Knows cars? Seems so.
You never checked any of it.
Check each one on its own.

thaler.name: Richard Thaler
thaler.did: Described the sunk cost trap in everyday spending in 1980 and won the 2017 Nobel prize for showing how people really decide.

arkes.name: Hal Arkes
arkes.did: With Catherine Blumer in 1985, showed that theatergoers who paid full price for season tickets went to more plays than those given a discount: the money already spent pulled them back.

festinger.name: Leon Festinger
festinger.did: Named cognitive dissonance in 1957, after studying a group whose prophecy of the end of the world failed and who then believed more strongly, not less.

aronson.name: Elliot Aronson
aronson.did: Showed in 1959 that people who went through a harsh initiation to join a dull group rated the group more highly: the cost made them defend the choice.

cialdini.name: Robert Cialdini
cialdini.did: Trained as a salesman undercover to study persuasion, and named scarcity, "only a few left", as one of its main levers in Influence (1984).

przybylski.name: Andrew Przybylski
przybylski.did: Built the first scale to measure fear of missing out in 2013 and found it ties to heavier social media use and lower mood.

wason.name: Peter Wason
wason.did: In 1960 asked people to find the rule behind the numbers 2, 4, 6. Most only tested numbers that fit their first guess, and never tried one that could prove it wrong.

nickerson.name: Raymond Nickerson
nickerson.did: Gathered the evidence for confirmation bias across science, law and medicine in one review (1998) that is still the standard account.

kahneman.name: Daniel Kahneman
kahneman.did: With Amos Tversky, mapped how judgment fails in predictable ways, from anchoring to loss aversion, and won the 2002 Nobel prize in economics for it.

tversky.name: Amos Tversky
tversky.did: With Daniel Kahneman, described the availability shortcut (1973), showed how framing flips choices (1981) and built prospect theory (1979), which measured that losses weigh about twice as much as equal gains.

northcraft.name: Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale
northcraft.did: In 1987 showed that real estate agents valued the same house higher or lower depending on the asking price they were shown, while saying the price had not swayed them.

slovic.name: Paul Slovic
slovic.did: Spent decades measuring how people judge risk, and showed that dread and vivid images, not the numbers, drive what we fear.

asch.name: Solomon Asch
asch.did: In the 1950s had people match line lengths beside actors giving a wrong answer. About a third of the time, people went along with the group against their own eyes.

shiller.name: Robert Shiller
shiller.did: Warned of the dot-com and housing bubbles before they burst by showing how prices feed on the crowd's own excitement, and won the 2013 Nobel prize in economics.

samuelson.name: William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser
samuelson.did: Named status quo bias in 1988, showing in experiments and real choices of health plans that people stick with whatever option is already theirs.

madrian.name: Brigitte Madrian
madrian.did: With Dennis Shea (2001), showed that when one company made retirement savings the default, joining went from about a third of new workers to most of them.

mcneil.name: Barbara McNeil
mcneil.did: In 1982 showed that doctors and patients chose surgery far more often when its risks were given as the chance of surviving than as the chance of dying, with the same numbers.

regan.name: Dennis Regan
regan.did: In 1971 had a stranger give people a free soda, then ask them to buy raffle tickets. They bought about twice as many as people given nothing, liked or not.

milgram.name: Stanley Milgram
milgram.did: In 1963 showed that about two in three ordinary people kept giving what they believed were dangerous shocks when a calm man in a lab coat told them to go on.

hofling.name: Charles Hofling
hofling.did: In 1966 had an unknown "doctor" phone hospital nurses to give twice the maximum dose of a drug. 21 of 22 nurses were stopped on the way to give it.

worchel.name: Stephen Worchel
worchel.did: In 1975 offered people the same cookie from a jar of ten or a jar of two. The cookie from the nearly empty jar was rated more desirable.

fischhoff.name: Baruch Fischhoff
fischhoff.did: In 1975 showed that people told how a historical event turned out believed they would have predicted it, and could not undo the knowledge when asked to.

dunning.name: David Dunning and Justin Kruger
dunning.did: In 1999 found that people who scored lowest on tests of logic and grammar rated themselves well above average: the skill to do it is the skill to judge it.

svenson.name: Ola Svenson
svenson.did: In 1981 asked drivers to rate their own skill. Most American drivers in the study put themselves in the safest, most skilled half.

buehler.name: Roger Buehler
buehler.did: In 1994, with Dale Griffin and Michael Ross, asked students when they would finish their theses. They guessed about 34 days; it took about 56.

flyvbjerg.name: Bent Flyvbjerg
flyvbjerg.did: Studied thousands of big building projects and found that about nine in ten run over budget, over time, or both.

skinner.name: B. F. Skinner
skinner.did: Showed with animals that rewards given at random keep behavior going far longer than rewards given every time.

schull.name: Natasha Dow Schüll
schull.did: Spent years in Las Vegas studying how slot machines are designed to keep people playing, in Addiction by Design (2012).

thorndike.name: Edward Thorndike
thorndike.did: Named the halo effect in 1920, after finding that army officers who rated a soldier well on looks also rated him well on intelligence and loyalty.

nisbett.name: Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson
nisbett.did: In 1977 showed students the same lecturer acting warm or cold. Warm, his looks and accent were rated appealing; cold, irritating. The students denied his manner swayed them.

channels.name: Social Psychology (UC Berkeley, Sociology 150A)
channels.what: A full Berkeley course: cognitive biases, conformity, obedience, identity. The lectures behind many units here.

channels.name: Crash Course Psychology
channels.what: 40 short episodes on how the mind works, including how memory, thinking and judgment go wrong.
